findings.requirement_type: D&O Entity Coverage — Manufacturing & Professional Services Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Contract requirements not provided in this audit. Industry-standard expectation: D&O entity coverage to respond to claims by clients/counterparties arising from product defects or service failures, particularly for PE-backed companies with regulatory exposure.
findings.contract_page: N/A — contract insurance provisions not provided
findings.contract_file: Redacted12.11.24_City and County of Los Angeles California Renewal_Fully Executed.pdf (amendment only — base contract not provided)
findings.policy_quote: Adds exclusion to ALL D&O Insuring Agreements for Claims arising from: (1) product malfunction, defect, or deficiency in design/manufacture; OR (2) rendering of (or failure to render) any services for others for a fee, including services for customers or clients. Exceptions: (i) civil proceedings brought by security holders in their capacity as such without instigation by an Insured Entity or Manager; OR (ii) Derivative Actions/Demands.
findings.gap_description: The Hartford Management Liability policy contains a manufacturing AND professional services exclusion that bars Insuring Agreement C (Entity Liability) coverage for any claim arising from product defects (ballot printing/election hardware) OR services rendered for a fee (election processing, mail sorting, technology services). Runbeck's entire revenue stream falls inside both prongs. A county lawsuit alleging defective ballot software, election failure, or service breakdown would trigger this exclusion at the entity level. Coverage survives only for: (a) shareholder derivative actions or (b) individual director/officer protection (Insuring Agreements A and B).
findings.plain_english: Your D&O policy says: if a county sues your company because a ballot system failed or you didn't deliver election services correctly, the company itself is NOT covered. Only the individual directors and officers are covered, and only if shareholders sue. This is the worst possible exclusion for your business model — it carves out the exact lawsuit you're most likely to face. A single contested election going wrong could produce a multi-million-dollar entity claim with no D&O response.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate removal or material narrowing of PP 00 H350 at renewal. If carrier won't budge, secure standalone Tech E&O entity-level wrapper or place D&O with a different carrier that does not impose this exclusion on election services risks. This should be the #1 marketing issue at renewal.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partial — Gemini Professional Liability ($5M post-4/1/2021) covers service errors but NOT D&O claims (board mismanagement, M&A, regulatory enforcement against directors). PL responds to E&O claims; not a substitute for entity D&O.
discoveryQuestions: If a county sued your company tomorrow because a ballot printing batch had a defect that delayed a runoff election, who would defend the company — and who would pay the settlement?

Your PE sponsors put you on a board with fiduciary duties to multiple stakeholders. Has anyone walked you through what happens if a regulatory agency investigates the company itself, not the individual directors?
When the LA County contract or any other large county RFP requires evidence of D&O coverage for the entity, does your current policy actually deliver what you'd represent?
Have you ever modeled what a contested-election lawsuit would cost — in defense fees alone — over 18 months of litigation?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Social Engineering / Cyber Deception Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard requirement: meaningful social engineering / business email compromise coverage for vendors handling government payments and sensitive election infrastructure.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception sublimit: $250,000. Cyber Deception retention: $250,000.
findings.gap_description: AmTrust Cyber sublimits social engineering/cyber deception at $250,000 with a $250,000 retention. Net effective coverage is ZERO until losses exceed retention — and the entire policy ceiling is the same number as the deductible. This structure is functionally a non-coverage. Compounding the problem: the Hanover Commercial Package Crime extension (411-0793, pg 84) only covers BEC where a software contractor causes the fraud; standard CFO/vendor impersonation BEC is excluded. The Management Liability Crime part covers Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud at $2M but Deception Fraud at only $15,000 (Hartford pg 47, $5,000 retention). Across the entire program, there is no meaningful coverage for a CFO email-impersonation wire-fraud event.
findings.plain_english: You're a government vendor processing wires and ACH for county contracts. The most common cyberattack today — a fraudster sends a fake email pretending to be your CEO or a county official telling Accounts Payable to wire money — would not be covered by any policy in your program in any meaningful way. Your cyber policy says they'll pay up to $250K, but you have to pay the first $250K. So unless you lose more than $250K AND you have $250K of pure profit to throw at it, the policy pays you nothing. This is the single most likely cyber loss your industry faces, and you're effectively self-insured for it.
findings.recommendation: Restructure cyber deception terms at renewal: target $1M sublimit with $25K-$50K retention. If AmTrust won't restructure, market the cyber renewal — multiple carriers (Coalition, At-Bay, Beazley) offer $1M social engineering with reasonable retentions. Implement dual-control wire authorization protocols and document them for underwriter credit.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No — Hanover Crime extension (pg 84) covers software-contractor BEC only; Hartford Crime Deception Fraud is $15K sublimit. No other policy responds.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through how a wire transfer over $50K gets approved at your company today. How many people see it before it goes out the door?
Have you or anyone on your finance team ever received an email that looked like it was from the CEO or a county client asking for an unusual payment?
If a fraudster impersonated a county procurement officer and tricked your AP team into wiring $400,000 to a fake bank account, how much of that would you recover from insurance?
What controls do you have for verifying changes to vendor banking information mid-contract?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Network Security & Privacy Breach Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for an election technology vendor handling voter PII for 90M+ registrants: meaningful first-party and third-party privacy/network security coverage with no PL carve-out.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes from Professional Liability coverage: (1) any claim arising from network security or privacy breach — defined broadly to include failure to handle/manage/store/destroy confidential or PII, violations of insured's privacy policy, violations of FTC Act §5(a), CA SB 1386, DPPA, Gramm-Leach-Bliley, HIPAA, and any similar state/federal identity theft or privacy protection statute, and failure to protect against unauthorized access/denial-of-service/malicious code transmission... Additionally amends Loss definition to exclude notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, forensic expenses, PR expenses, fines, and penalties arising from unauthorized access to or disclosure of confidential/personal information.
findings.gap_description: The Gemini Professional Liability policy expressly carves out all privacy/network-security claims from PL coverage. AmTrust Cyber is intended to fill this gap — but at only $4M aggregate with defense costs eroding limits and shared across first-party AND third-party. For a company processing voter data for 90M+ registrants across 31 states, $4M is undersized given regulatory penalty exposure (state AGs, FTC, potential class actions under CCPA/state privacy laws) and forensic/notification cost stacks. The PL policy's exception clause does state that if a Cyber Coverage Endorsement is attached to the PL itself, the exclusion does not apply to that endorsement — but no such endorsement appears in the policy.
findings.plain_english: You handle voter data for 90 million Americans. If that data gets breached — by hack, employee error, lost laptop, or vendor failure — your professional liability policy says 'not our problem.' All of the cleanup work (notifying voters, hiring forensics teams, responding to state attorneys general, defending class actions) has to come out of your $4M cyber policy, which also has to cover defense costs and any business interruption. A meaningful breach on a presidential election cycle could blow through that $4M in the first 90 days on forensics and notification alone, before any lawsuits are filed.
findings.recommendation: Increase Cyber aggregate to $10M minimum at renewal; consider $15M-$25M given client base. Push for defense outside limits or a separate defense-cost bucket. Confirm no Cyber Coverage Endorsement exists on the Gemini PL — if one was intended, get it issued. Consider a cyber excess tower above AmTrust to align with the $10M umbrella tower on other lines.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber ($4M aggregate) — but limit is undersized for the exposure and excludes Hanover GL/Umbrella from responding (multiple cyber/data exclusions on those policies).
discoveryQuestions: If a hostile actor accessed your voter registration database the week before a presidential election, what's your first call — and what does that conversation cost you in the first 30 days?
How many voter records does Runbeck touch in a federal election cycle, and what does state-by-state notification cost work out to per record under the strictest privacy laws?
Have you priced what a BIPA or CCPA class action defense looks like at the major law firms, and how that compares to your $4M cyber tower?
Does your PE sponsor know that your cyber tower is one-tenth of your management liability tower for a risk that's at least 10× more likely?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Mail Processing Services Restricted Retroactive Date
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for claims-made coverage on a core, ongoing service line: prior acts coverage matched to the date the service began.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #1 (VP 07 84 07 17) applies a LATER retroactive date of 04/01/2021 exclusively to 'outbound and inbound mail processing services.' Claims arising from mail processing errors prior to 04/01/2021 have zero coverage under this policy.
findings.gap_description: While the base PL retroactive date is 03/27/2017, mail processing services — described in the company profile as a core revenue line — has a separate retro date of 04/01/2021. Any claim alleging a mail processing error from 2017-2020 (e.g., misdirected ballots, late ballot delivery, processing errors discovered post-election) is uninsured. Claims-made policies trigger on when the claim is reported, but the underlying wrongful act must occur after the retroactive date. With a 4-year prior acts gap on this core service, late-emerging claims (a county discovers a 2020 election processing error in 2026) would have no coverage.
findings.plain_english: Mail processing — sorting and handling ballots — is one of your three biggest revenue streams. Your professional liability policy covers errors from this service only if they happened on or after April 1, 2021. Anything before that is uninsured, even if you only just got sued for it. Election-related claims often surface years after the fact — a county's auditor finds something, a losing candidate sues, a state recount uncovers an error. If a 2020 election claim hits you in 2026, your PL policy says no coverage.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate to align the mail processing retro date with the base 03/27/2017 retro date at renewal. If carrier won't budge on a 4-year backdated retro, document that any mail processing claim with pre-2021 wrongful acts must be self-funded and quantify reserves. Consider a tail/ERP for the prior carrier covering 2017-2021 mail processing if one existed.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No other policy in program covers professional services E&O.
discoveryQuestions: Mail processing is one of your largest service lines — how many counties were you serving for ballot mail in 2018, 2019, and 2020?
If a county discovered today that a 2019 ballot batch was mishandled and missed deadlines, what does your contract with them say about your liability and the time limit for claims?
Why does your mail processing have a different retroactive date than your other services — was that a carrier underwriting decision, and was it negotiated?
Have you had any disputes with counties post-2017 over mail handling that were resolved without a formal claim being filed?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Ransomware / Extortion Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard requirement for technology services vendors: ransomware/extortion coverage adequate to ransom demand averages plus business interruption.
findings.policy_quote: Technology Services Extension (Endorsement #6) excludes: hardware malfunction, electrical failure, extortion/ransomware (CRITICAL gap for election tech company), delay in performance/delivery, ISP outage, and funds transfer/loss.
findings.gap_description: The PL Technology Services Extension expressly excludes extortion, blackmail, ransom payments, and private security costs. Election technology companies are top-tier ransomware targets due to time-sensitive operations (ransom paid quickly to restore systems before election day) and political visibility. AmTrust Cyber covers Ransom Payment at $4M, which is the only mitigation — but defense costs erode that limit and it's shared with other first-party coverages.
findings.plain_english: Ransomware is the #1 cyber threat to election infrastructure right now. Your professional liability policy excludes it entirely. Your cyber policy covers it up to $4 million — but that same $4 million also has to cover business interruption, data restoration, breach notification, lawsuits, and regulatory fines. If you got hit with a $1.5M ransom demand 10 days before a federal election, you'd pay it (because you can't afford the downtime) and then have $2.5M left for everything else. A second incident in the same year would have nothing.
findings.recommendation: Increase Cyber aggregate to $10M minimum, with separate ransomware sublimit at $5M+. Implement and document offline backups, segmented networks, and incident response retainer for underwriter credit. Verify carrier's ransom payment workflow and OFAC screening process pre-loss.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber Ransom Payment $4M (aggregate, not per occurrence) — undersized given exposure and shared with all other first-party coverages.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware actor encrypted your ballot processing systems 14 days before a presidential election and demanded $2 million, how do you decide whether to pay, and who's on that decision call?
What's your recovery time objective for ballot processing systems if you have to rebuild from offline backups?
Have you done a tabletop exercise with your incident response retainer firm specifically for an election-cycle ransomware scenario?
Does your AmTrust cyber policy require pre-approval before paying a ransom, and what's the OFAC screening turnaround they need?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Split Limits of Liability Tower
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: declared $5M/$5M limits available for all covered claims arising from acts after the retroactive date.
findings.policy_quote: Effective structure is tiered by date of Wrongful Act: (1) Acts on/after 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate. (2) Additional $1M excess of $1M for acts on/after 09/06/2019 (total $2M/$2M). (3) Additional $3M excess of $2M for acts on/after 04/01/2021 (total $5M/$5M). Full $5M limits only available for wrongful acts occurring after 04/01/2021.
findings.gap_description: The declared $5M/$5M limits on the dec page are misleading. A claim arising from a wrongful act between 12/1/2007 and 9/5/2019 is capped at $1M. A claim from 9/6/2019 to 3/31/2021 is capped at $2M. The full $5M only applies to acts after 4/1/2021. The Convex excess sits over $5M — meaning for older claims, there is a $4M coverage corridor where neither primary nor excess responds. Election claims often surface years after the wrongful act (election results challenged, audits performed, FOIA requests revealing errors).
findings.plain_english: Your policy says $5 million on the cover page, but read the fine print — that $5 million only applies if the screw-up happened after April 1, 2021. For anything before that, your real limit is $1 million or $2 million. So a 2018 ballot processing error that gets discovered and sued in 2026 has a $1 million ceiling, with $4 million of unfunded exposure between your primary and your excess policy.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to flatten the tower so $5M applies to all acts post-retroactive date. If carrier resists, accept the structure but quantify the prior-acts liability reserves on the balance sheet and disclose to PE sponsors. Verify Convex excess attaches at $1M for older acts (which it likely does not — it attaches at $5M flat per dec page, leaving the corridor).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Convex excess (XPL000040-0425) attaches at $5M; for sub-$5M tower acts, no excess drop-down.
discoveryQuestions: Were the split limits in your professional liability policy disclosed and explained to your PE sponsors when this policy was bound?
How far back does your contract with LA County or other major counties allow them to bring claims against you for past services?
If a 2019 election error became the basis for a $3 million lawsuit today, do you understand how much of that your insurance would actually pay?
Has your broker walked you through the gap between your primary $1M-$2M for older acts and the Convex excess attaching at $5M?

findings.requirement_type: Excess Tower — Convex Policy Number Documentation Defect
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: excess policy must reference the correct underlying primary policy number to attach validly.
findings.policy_quote: Policy number on Declarations Page Item 5 (VIPL056495) does not match the Schedule of Underlying Insurance XPL-301 (VIPL055885). These are different policy numbers.
findings.gap_description: The Convex Excess Tech E&O Declarations Item 5 identifies the Followed Policy as Gemini VIPL056495. The Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301) lists Gemini VIPL055885. Different policy numbers. If these reference different policies, the $5M excess layer either does not validly attach OR follows the wrong policy. In a claims scenario, Convex could decline coverage on the basis that the named underlying policy was not maintained.
findings.plain_english: Your $5 million excess policy and your $5 million primary policy don't agree on the policy number they're built around. This is a documentation defect that could let your excess carrier walk away from a $5M-$10M claim. It's almost certainly a typo — but in insurance, typos in policy numbers are not 'almost certainly' fixed when the carrier wants to deny coverage. This needs an endorsement correction this week, not at renewal.
findings.recommendation: Immediately email RSG Specialty and Convex requesting a corrected Schedule of Underlying Insurance endorsement reflecting the actual primary policy number. Get written confirmation from both Gemini and Convex that they agree on which policy is the followed policy. Document in writing.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: N/A — the issue IS the excess policy attachment.
discoveryQuestions: Has your broker reconciled all policy numbers across your professional liability tower since the Gemini renewal?
If Convex denied a $7M claim citing the policy number mismatch, what's your contractual recourse against the broker who placed it?
Do you have a written confirmation from RSG Specialty that the excess policy follows the correct primary?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Professional Liability, Cyber, and D&O Excluded
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a $10M umbrella on a PE-backed company with $90M+ voter data exposure: meaningful excess coverage above primary management/cyber/professional towers.
findings.policy_quote: Coverage A excludes 'any liability or expense arising out of the rendering of or failure to render any professional service' [475-0031, pg 46]; Coverage B (built-in) excludes professional services, D&O, employment-related practices, and cyber. Forms 475-0654, 475-0655, 475-0661 add absolute exclusions for Access/Disclosure of Confidential Information, Violation of Data Privacy Laws (BIPA/CCPA/GDPR), and Cyber Incident — applicable to BOTH Coverage A and Coverage B.
findings.gap_description: The Hanover Commercial Umbrella ($10M) is a follow-form excess for GL, Auto, WC, and EBL ONLY. It does NOT sit over Professional Liability, Cyber, D&O, or EPLI. Worse, even Coverage B (the standalone umbrella drop-down) excludes professional services, cyber, data privacy, D&O, and discrimination. Effect: the company has $10M of excess capacity for slip-and-fall/auto/WC, but ZERO umbrella capacity for the actual primary risks of an election technology company (E&O, cyber, management liability). Cyber tower tops out at $4M. ML tower tops out at $2M D&O / $1M EPLI / $1M Fiduciary. PL tower tops out at $10M (with split limits issues). For a PE-backed company processing data for 90M+ voters, this is profoundly mis-sized.
findings.plain_english: You have a $10 million umbrella, which sounds great until you realize what it actually does. It backs up your auto policy, your general liability, and workers' comp. It does NOT back up the four policies that actually matter for your business: professional liability, cyber, D&O, and EPLI. So if a county sues you for $8M alleging election failure, your umbrella sits there doing nothing — only your $5M primary and $5M Convex excess respond. If the claim is $15M, you write a $5M check from corporate cash. Your umbrella is sized for risks you don't really have, and absent for the risks you do have.
findings.recommendation: Build a proper excess tower ABOVE the management liability and cyber primaries: target $5M-$10M excess D&O, $5M-$10M excess Cyber, $5M-$10M excess EPLI. The Hanover umbrella structure is appropriate for the GL/Auto/WC piece but does not address the company's actual loss profile. Get quotes for: Excess D&O over Hartford, Excess Cyber over AmTrust, and Excess EPLI over Hartford.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: PL excess tower exists ($10M total via Convex); no excess D&O, Cyber, or EPLI.
discoveryQuestions: If a class action under California's privacy law named your company for $25 million, where in your $10 million umbrella does that money come from?
Your PE sponsors carry their own D&O — but if a regulatory enforcement action seeks $5 million from the company, your D&O tower stops at $2 million. What's the plan for the next $3 million?

What's the largest single claim, in dollars, that you could realistically face from a county, a voter class action, or a state AG — and how does that number compare to your actual coverage on each line?
Has your broker shown you a tower diagram side-by-side: the lines where you have $10M of umbrella above primary, versus the lines where you have $0 of umbrella?

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability — Biometric Identifiers Exclusion (BIPA / State Equivalents)
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: meaningful coverage for biometric privacy statutes for vendors using voter ID verification, signature matching, or biometric authentication.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes any claim arising from violations of statutes regulating biometric identifiers or biometric information (fingerprints, retina scans, face geometry, voiceprints, etc.).
findings.gap_description: BIPA (Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act) carries statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation and $5,000 per intentional/reckless violation, per person. With 90M+ voter records and election-cycle signature verification, even an inadvertent practice violation could trigger 8-figure aggregate exposure in a single state. The PL policy excludes this entirely. The Hanover GL also excludes via CG 00 69 (data privacy law exclusion expressly naming BIPA). The Umbrella also excludes (475-0655). The only potential coverage is the AmTrust Cyber regulatory defense and fines limit ($4M shared aggregate).
findings.plain_english: Illinois has a law called BIPA. If you use voter signature matching or any biometric verification (face, fingerprint, voice) on Illinois voters, and your privacy disclosures aren't perfectly compliant, every single voter record is worth $1,000-$5,000 in statutory damages in a class action. You serve millions of voters. The math gets uncomfortable fast. Your PL policy, GL policy, and umbrella all say no coverage. Only your $4 million cyber policy might respond — and BIPA settlements have crossed $200 million in recent cases.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether biometric processing occurs and in which states. If yes, place standalone biometric/privacy liability cover (specialty market). Ensure consent forms and retention policies meet BIPA/CCPA/state biometric statute requirements. Consider increasing Cyber regulatory defense limits significantly.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber regulatory defense and fines included in $4M shared aggregate — undersized for class-action BIPA exposure.
discoveryQuestions: Do any of your election technology products use signature matching, facial recognition, or voiceprint verification — even indirectly through a county client's workflow?
Are you familiar with BIPA and the recent settlements running into the hundreds of millions?
Which states do you process biometric data in, and have you reviewed each state's biometric privacy law for compliance with your privacy disclosures?
If a class action under BIPA covered 100,000 Illinois voters, do you understand that even at the lower statutory rate, that's a $100 million theoretical exposure?

findings.requirement_type: General Liability — Classification Limitation on Arch Policy
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: GL coverage applies to all operations of the named insured, not a narrow subset of classifications.
findings.policy_quote: Coverage applies ONLY to operations for which a classification is listed on the declarations. Classified operations are: (1) Alarms and Alarm Systems – Installation (Code 91127), (2) Detective or Investigative Agencies – Private (Code 91636), and (3) Security and Patrol Agencies (Code 98751, $190,000 payroll exposure).
findings.gap_description: The Arch policy is a SECURITY GUARD GL with $1M/$3M limits. Its Classification Limitation expressly restricts coverage to security/alarm/detective operations only. Runbeck's CORE operations (election technology, ballot printing, mail processing, software development) are NOT covered under this policy. Coverage for those operations exists under the Hanover Commercial Package GL ($1M/$2M). It is unclear from this audit why Runbeck holds a separate security guard GL — possibly relating to in-house election-day security or a specific subsidiary operation. If contracts require GL coverage for election services, the Arch policy does NOT respond; only the Hanover policy does.
findings.plain_english: You actually have two GL policies. The Arch one only covers security guard operations — alarms, patrols, investigations. It does NOT cover election technology, ballot printing, or mail processing — your actual business. Those are covered under your Hanover commercial package. This isn't necessarily a problem, but if anyone is presenting the Arch policy to counties as your election services GL, that would be a serious misrepresentation. Make sure all certificates of insurance for election-services work cite the Hanover policy.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with management WHY a separate security guard GL exists — is there a security subsidiary, an in-house guard force, or election-day security operations? If the Arch policy was accidentally placed and Runbeck has no security guard operations, cancel and recover unearned premium. If legitimately needed, ensure COIs for election services work cite the Hanover policy only. Audit recently-issued certificates.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Commercial Package GL (ZB4 H221415 05) covers election services, ballot printing, mail processing operations.
discoveryQuestions: Why does Runbeck carry a separate security guard general liability policy with Arch — is there an in-house security force, or is this for an election-day patrol operation?
Have you reviewed recent certificates of insurance issued to counties to confirm the right GL policy is being cited?
Is there a subsidiary entity that performs guard or detective work, and is that entity properly named on the Arch policy?
If a county claim arose from a ballot processing error, you understand the Arch policy would not respond — correct?

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Compensation — Waiver of Subrogation Gap (GA, NC, IL)
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard government contract requirement: blanket Waiver of Subrogation on WC policies for all states where the contractor has employees performing work.
findings.policy_quote: Waiver applies to Business Auto Coverage Form. Subrogation waived only to the extent it was waived prior to the accident or loss under a written contract. Applies in states: AZ, AR, CO, FL, IN, MN, NY, OR, PA. [GA, NC, IL not listed]
findings.gap_description: Blanket WOS endorsement covers AZ, AR, CO, FL, IN, MN, NY, OR, PA — but NOT GA, NC, or IL. Premium discount endorsements confirm active WC payroll exposure in all three excluded states. CA is covered separately via WC 04 03 06. If county or government contracts in GA, NC, or IL require WOS on the WC policy (common for government work), the policy does not deliver, and a contractual breach could occur if a certificate of insurance with WOS language is issued falsely.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp policy has a blanket waiver of subrogation that applies in 9 states plus California separately — but not in Georgia, North Carolina, or Illinois, where you also have employees. If you have county contracts in any of those three states that require a waiver of subrogation, your policy doesn't actually deliver it. Issuing certificates that claim it does could be a contractual misrepresentation.
findings.recommendation: Endorse WC 00 03 13 to add GA, NC, IL to the list of waiver states. This is a no-cost or low-cost endorsement (additional premium charged only if specific contracts trigger). Audit current COIs to confirm no certificates are claiming WOS in those three states without endorsement support.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: WC waivers must be on the WC policy itself; no other policy substitutes.
discoveryQuestions: How many active county or state contracts do you have in Georgia, North Carolina, and Illinois right now?
Have any of those contracts asked for waiver of subrogation language on workers' comp specifically?
When you issue certificates of insurance to those three states, what policy language is being represented to the county?
Has anyone audited your COI templates against your actual policy endorsements in the last 12 months?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Electronic Data Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a technology-driven business: meaningful first-party coverage for loss/corruption of electronic data.
findings.policy_quote: Electronic Data Additional Coverage capped at $2,500 per policy year regardless of number of occurrences or premises.
findings.policy_page: Page 143, CP 00 10 10 12; Page 157, CP 00 30 (Interruption of Computer Operations $2,500 sublimit)
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO BPP and BI forms cap electronic data at $2,500/year and Interruption of Computer Operations at $2,500/year — token amounts for a company whose entire product is electronic data (ballot files, voter records, programming). Equipment Breakdown Data Restoration ($100K) provides additional coverage but only triggered by mechanical breakdown, not cyber events. AmTrust Cyber covers data restoration for cyber incidents within its $4M aggregate.
findings.plain_english: Your property policy treats your most valuable asset — election data — as worth $2,500. For a $20+ million-revenue technology company, that's not coverage, it's a punchline. Your cyber policy covers data restoration for cyberattacks, but mechanical/non-cyber data loss has only token coverage. If a server farm gets damaged by a non-cyber event, you'd be reconstructing voter files largely on your own dime.
findings.recommendation: Increase Electronic Data and Interruption of Computer Operations sublimits to $250K-$500K each at next renewal. Hanover should have a Premium Choice or similar endorsement option. If not, marketing the property line is warranted.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber Data and System Recovery $4M (cyber-triggered only); Equipment Breakdown Data Restoration $100K (mechanical-triggered only).
discoveryQuestions: If a fire at your Phoenix headquarters destroyed your primary servers and your backup tapes were partially damaged, what does it cost to reconstruct ballot files for an upcoming election?
Are your data and server replacement costs reflected in any property limit, or are they only addressed by cyber and equipment breakdown?
What's the value, in business interruption alone, of one week of downtime in your election processing systems during a federal cycle?

findings.requirement_type: California Employers' Liability — Labor Code §2810.3 Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard requirement: EL coverage for joint employer liability in states with labor contractor statutes.
findings.policy_quote: Employers Liability coverage excludes liability arising from CA Labor Code Section 2810.3 (labor contractor client liability).
findings.gap_description: California Labor Code §2810.3 imposes joint and several liability on client employers (Runbeck) for labor contractor failures, including WC obligations. The endorsement excludes EL coverage for such joint liability. If Runbeck uses staffing firms or labor contractors for CA election operations (ballot processing, equipment deployment), and the contractor fails to maintain WC, Runbeck would be jointly liable but uninsured under Part Two.
findings.plain_english: California has a law that holds you responsible if your staffing vendor fails to carry workers' comp for their workers on your jobs. Your policy specifically excludes this exposure. If you use temp agencies in California — and you almost certainly do during election cycles — and that agency's coverage lapses, you could be on the hook for an injured worker's lifetime medical and indemnity benefits with zero insurance.
findings.recommendation: Audit California labor contractor relationships. Require COIs from staffing vendors and verify currency monthly during active engagements. Add contractual indemnification language naming Runbeck as additional insured on staffing vendor's WC. Consider Alternate Employer endorsement with carrier.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No — staffing vendor's own WC policy if maintained, but uninsured if vendor lapses.
discoveryQuestions: How many staffing or temp agencies did you use in California during the 2024 election cycle?
Do you collect and verify workers' compensation certificates from those staffing vendors monthly during active engagements?
If a temp worker assigned by an agency to your Sacramento operation got injured, and the agency's WC lapsed, who pays for the lifetime medical?
Is there an Alternate Employer endorsement on your WC policy, or one available, for California staffing relationships?

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Split Prior/Pending Date on Excess Layer
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: uniform prior/pending date across the entire D&O tower.
findings.policy_quote: The base $1,000,000 layer retains the standard prior/pending date of 8/18/2023. The additional $1,000,000 excess of the first $1,000,000 has a later prior/pending date of 04/02/2024 — meaning the second million of D&O coverage excludes claims based on wrongful acts known or pending before 04/02/2024.
findings.gap_description: The D&O excess layer has a later prior/pending date than the primary ($1M) layer — 7.5 months shorter retroactive reach. Claims arising from wrongful acts between 8/18/2023 and 4/1/2024 are covered up to $1M only; the excess $1M does not respond. For a PE-backed company with ongoing regulatory and stakeholder activity, this 7.5-month window of half-coverage is a concrete exposure.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O policy says you have $2 million of coverage. But for any wrongdoing that happened between mid-August 2023 and early April 2024, you actually only have $1 million. The second million has a later start date. So if a 2023 board decision triggers a 2026 lawsuit asking for $1.8 million, you cover the first million from D&O and write a $800K check from corporate cash.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to align the excess layer's prior/pending date with the primary's 8/18/2023 date. If carrier won't budge, document the 7.5-month window in board materials and ensure no known potential claims fall in that window.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No — D&O is the only coverage for these claims.
discoveryQuestions: Were any board decisions, regulatory inquiries, or stakeholder disputes underway between August 2023 and April 2024 that could later become a claim?
Did your PE sponsors execute any transactions, board changes, or recapitalizations in that 7.5-month window?
Has anyone walked your CFO through what 'split prior and pending date' actually means on your policy?

findings.requirement_type: Defense Costs Inside Limits — Cyber, ML, PL
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard preference for high-stakes liability lines: defense costs outside or in addition to limits.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber: 'Defense costs erode the $4M aggregate limit of liability.' Management Liability: 'No Defense Outside the Limit election visible.' Professional Liability: 'Claim Expenses reduce and may exhaust the Each Claim and Aggregate Limits.'
findings.policy_page: AmTrust Dec; Hartford pg 13; Gemini pg 1
findings.gap_description: Across all three core specialty liability policies (Cyber, ML, PL), defense costs erode policy limits. For an election technology company facing complex, prolonged litigation (election lawsuits average 18-36 months), defense cost burn is severe. A $4M cyber limit could be largely consumed by forensics, regulatory defense, and class action defense before any indemnity is paid.
findings.plain_english: On three of your most important policies, the lawyers' fees come out of the same bucket as the settlement money. If a class action runs for two years and burns $2 million in legal fees, you only have $2 million left to actually pay the plaintiffs. Election cases tend to be long and expensive — defense outside limits is worth real money in this sector.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request defense outside limits or a separate defense bucket on Cyber and ML. PL likely cannot be moved off DIL but the impact can be reduced by raising aggregate limits. Quote both options with carriers.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: N/A
discoveryQuestions: If a class action burns $1.8 million in defense costs over 24 months, how much of your $4 million cyber limit do you have left to settle?
Have you priced what 'defense outside limits' would add to your premium versus the limit erosion you'd accept by saying no?
What's your cost-per-month exposure during a contested-election lawsuit at top-tier defense firms?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Care, Custody, or Control Exclusion (Ballot Transit)
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a transporter of high-value, time-sensitive election materials: coverage for property in transit.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes property damage to property owned or transported by the insured or in the insured's care, custody or control (except sidetrack agreements).
findings.gap_description: The auto policy excludes damage to property in the insured's care, custody, or control. Runbeck transports ballots and election equipment (high value, time-sensitive). If a vehicle accident damages or destroys ballots in transit, the auto policy will not respond. The Hanover Commercial Package property coverage includes Business Personal Property In Transit ($100K) and Property Off Premises ($250K) — partial mitigation. The Auto Broadening Endorsement Item 13 provides only $500 for audio/visual/data electronic equipment.
findings.plain_english: If your truck rolls over and ballots are destroyed mid-transit, your auto policy doesn't pay because the cargo is in your care, custody, and control. Your property policy picks up part of it ($100K transit, $250K off-premises) — but for a major election cycle that's not enough. And if it's actual election technology equipment damaged in the rollover, the auto policy gives you $500.
findings.recommendation: Increase Property In Transit limit to at least $500K. Consider scheduled Inland Marine cargo policy specifically for election season transports. For high-value equipment routes, document and schedule specifically.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover property In Transit $100K, Off Premises $250K — undersized for election cycle peaks.
discoveryQuestions: What's the dollar value of the largest single ballot or equipment shipment you move during a federal election cycle?
If a Sprinter van rolled over and destroyed 200,000 printed ballots three weeks before election day, how much does that cost in reprinting, expedited shipping, and potential election delay claims?
Have you ever calculated peak in-transit values during a presidential election week?
Are your high-value routes ever consolidated in single trucks, or are they split for risk reasons?

findings.requirement_type: Crime — Computer & Funds Transfer Fraud / Social Engineering
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: meaningful coverage for funds transfer fraud, computer fraud, and social engineering.
findings.policy_quote: Hartford Crime — Deception Fraud sublimit $15,000 (pg 47). Hanover Property — Computer and Funds Transfer Fraud $50,000; social engineering coverage ONLY when caused by software contractor with written agreement.
findings.gap_description: Crime coverage across the program is fragmented and undersized for a $5-25M revenue government vendor. Hartford Crime: Computer Funds Transfer Fraud $2M, but Deception Fraud only $15K. Hanover property: $50K Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud, social engineering severely limited. AmTrust Cyber Deception: effectively $0 (see finding-002). Standard CFO-impersonation BEC has no meaningful coverage anywhere in program.
findings.plain_english: You have three policies that touch funds transfer fraud — and none of them cover the most common fraud type, where a fake email tricks someone into wiring money. Your cyber policy says they'll pay $250K but only after you eat $250K. Your management liability deception fraud is $15K. Your property fraud is $50K and only if a software contractor caused it. Add it up: meaningful BEC coverage is missing from your program.
findings.recommendation: Restructure across both Crime and Cyber to deliver a true $1M social engineering tower with reasonable retention. May require negotiating with both AmTrust (cyber) and Hartford (crime). Implement written wire authorization controls and dual signoff.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No meaningful coverage; see finding-002 for cyber detail.
discoveryQuestions: What's your single largest wire transfer in a typical election month?
How does a county client formally notify you of bank account changes for invoice payment?
Have you mapped your wire fraud exposure across crime, cyber, and property policies — and identified which one would actually pay?

findings.requirement_type: EPLI — Wage & Hour Defense Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a 50-200 employee multi-state operation: meaningful Wage & Hour defense coverage.
findings.policy_quote: Wage & Hour Violations are excluded from Damages. However, Defense Costs for Wage & Hour claims ARE covered up to the $100,000 Wage & Hour Defense Costs Sub-Limit. Actual damages/settlements remain uninsured.
findings.gap_description: EPLI provides only $100K Wage & Hour defense costs (no indemnity) and the insured has the duty to defend (not the carrier). For a 50-200 employee multi-state company across CA, NY, IL, OR, and other plaintiff-friendly W&H jurisdictions, $100K is consumed quickly in a single putative class action. Settlement/damages are entirely uninsured.
findings.plain_english: If a former employee filed a wage and hour class action — a very common claim type — your insurance pays for $100K of defense costs and zero damages. The company manages its own defense (the carrier won't even appoint a lawyer). $100K is what one lawyer at a firm bills in three months on a class action. Realistic exposure on a 100-person W&H class is $500K-$2M just to get to settlement.
findings.recommendation: Increase W&H defense sublimit to $250K-$500K at renewal. Audit timekeeping, exempt classifications, meal/rest break compliance especially in CA. Consider standalone wage & hour policy if exposure warrants.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No other policy covers W&H.
discoveryQuestions: How many California-based employees do you have, and what percentage are classified as exempt?
When was your last wage and hour audit by outside employment counsel?
If a former employee filed a putative class action alleging meal break violations across 60 California workers, what does defense cost in the first 12 months?
Do your timekeeping practices for election-cycle overtime hold up to a forensic audit?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Interruption of Computer Operations Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a technology business: meaningful business interruption coverage from electronic data destruction/corruption.
findings.policy_quote: $2,500 per policy year (unless Declarations show higher limit) for suspension caused by electronic data destruction/corruption.
findings.gap_description: Standard ISO BI form caps Interruption of Computer Operations at $2,500/year. For a technology-dependent operation with $11.5M total Business Income limit, this is a 1/4600 sublimit. AmTrust Cyber covers cyber-triggered BI within its $4M aggregate, but mechanical/property-triggered computer interruption is barely covered.
findings.plain_english: If a sprinkler discharge or HVAC failure damaged your data systems and shut down ballot processing for two weeks, your business income insurance pays $2,500. That's about 30 minutes of operations for a company your size. Your cyber policy only responds if the cause is cyber — a sprinkler isn't cyber.
findings.recommendation: Increase Interruption of Computer Operations sublimit to $1M-$2M at renewal. Hanover Premium Choice or similar should be available.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber BI $4M (cyber-triggered only); Equipment Breakdown BI (mechanical, full $11.5M limit).
discoveryQuestions: What's the per-day revenue and gross margin impact if your ballot processing systems went offline during peak election season?
Have you mapped which BI sublimit responds to which trigger — water damage, equipment breakdown, cyber, or pure data corruption?

findings.requirement_type: Per-Project Aggregate Cap Limitation
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation when servicing multiple county/government contracts: per-project aggregates without a policy cap.
findings.policy_quote: However, a Policy Aggregate Cap of $2,000,000 applies — this is the overall maximum regardless of number of locations or projects.
findings.gap_description: Per-project and per-location aggregates exist, but a $2M cap applies across ALL projects/locations combined (except Products/Completed Ops). For Runbeck simultaneously serving counties in 31 states during a federal election, multiple concurrent claims could exhaust the $2M cap quickly. The umbrella tower above provides $10M follow-form excess GL — significant additional capacity.
findings.plain_english: Your GL gives you separate aggregate limits for each project — but only up to $2 million total across the policy. So if you have multiple counties claiming damages in the same year, the sum can't exceed $2 million on the primary GL. Above that, your $10 million umbrella picks up — so in practice this is mainly a primary policy limit issue.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to remove or significantly increase the $2M policy aggregate cap. Confirm umbrella follow-form attaches at $2M for GL.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella $10M follow-form excess GL.
discoveryQuestions: How many simultaneous county contracts do you have active during a federal election cycle?
If three counties simultaneously alleged GL claims totaling $3M, do you understand how the $2M cap and umbrella interact?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Named Driver Exclusion (Malina Trujillo)
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: any insured driver should be covered, with non-driver designation managed operationally.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes all coverage for named individual MALINA TRUJILLO operating any covered auto, except Uninsured Motorist and Underinsured Motorist Coverage.
findings.gap_description: Named driver exclusion for Malina Trujillo. If this individual operates a covered auto and causes a loss, no coverage applies (except UM/UIM). Likely placed due to driver MVR issues. Operational management critical — keys/access must be controlled to prevent inadvertent operation.
findings.plain_english: There's a person named Malina Trujillo on your policy who's specifically excluded. If they get behind the wheel of a company car — even in an emergency — your auto policy won't cover the accident. You need to make sure this person never has access to a company vehicle, and HR/dispatch needs to know.
findings.recommendation: Verify operational controls preventing this individual from operating company vehicles. Document in HR records. Consider whether the underlying cause (likely MVR issue) has been resolved and the exclusion can be removed at renewal.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: No.
discoveryQuestions: Is Malina Trujillo a current employee, and if so, what role do they have?
What controls prevent this individual from accessing company vehicle keys?
Has the underlying issue that triggered this exclusion been resolved, and if so, can the exclusion be removed at renewal?

findings.requirement_type: PL Hammer Clause — Dual Structure (50/50 in SIR Context)
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: a single, predictable hammer clause structure.
findings.policy_quote: Within SIR context: hammer clause set at 50/50 — if insured refuses recommended settlement, company pays recommended amount + 100% of claim expenses incurred before refusal + 50% of claim expenses after refusal + 50% of covered loss above recommended amount.
findings.policy_page: Pages 33-34, Endorsement #11 (VP 06 99 07 17); Page 39, Endorsement #16 (VP 08 51 05 17 — 80/20 in deductible context)
findings.gap_description: PL has TWO hammer clauses with different splits depending on funding mechanism. Within the SIR ($25K), if the insured refuses a settlement Gemini recommends, the carrier's exposure caps at 50% above the refused settlement. In the deductible context, 80%. For a politically sensitive election services company that may have strong reputational reasons to fight rather than settle (e.g., a county alleging election fraud), the 50% hammer is severe.
findings.plain_english: If your insurance company recommends settling a lawsuit and you say no — for very legitimate reputational reasons — your share of any larger judgment goes from 0% to 50%. For an election company, the cases where you most want to fight (a baseless fraud allegation that would damage your reputation) are exactly the cases where you'd take the worst hammer hit.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push to consolidate to a single 80/20 hammer or eliminate the SIR/deductible distinction. Document a settlement-decision protocol involving CFO, GC, and CEO with insurance broker advisory.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: N/A
discoveryQuestions: Have you been in a position where you wanted to fight a baseless claim because the allegation alone would damage your reputation, and the carrier wanted to settle?
Do you have a written protocol for who makes the settle-or-fight call when reputation is involved?

findings.requirement_type: Carrier Concentration — E&S Surplus Lines on PL Tower
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: avoid same-carrier-group concentration across primary and excess on a single line.
findings.policy_quote: Gemini Insurance Company is a W.R. Berkley surplus lines carrier. Convex Insurance UK Limited is a non-admitted E&S carrier. Both the primary and excess are E&S placements.
findings.gap_description: Both primary PL (Gemini) and excess PL (Convex) are non-admitted E&S placements. AZ has no guaranty fund protection for either if insolvent. While not the same carrier group, neither benefits from admitted-market backstops. AmTrust Cyber is also E&S. Note: nothing inherently wrong with E&S placement (per CLAUDE.md rule 15) — flagged here as informational layered with carrier financial-strength verification recommendation.
findings.plain_english: Three of your most important policies — professional liability, excess professional, and cyber — are placed with non-admitted carriers. If any of them go bankrupt, Arizona's guaranty fund won't bail you out. The carriers themselves (W.R. Berkley group, Convex, AmTrust) have decent ratings, but verify AM Best ratings annually and watch financial-strength downgrades.
findings.recommendation: Verify current AM Best ratings annually; subscribe to ratings alerts. Document in renewal file. Consider whether admitted-market PL is available at competitive terms (likely not for election tech specialty, which is why E&S exists).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: N/A
discoveryQuestions: Do you receive AM Best rating change alerts for your PL and Cyber carriers?
What's your protocol if any carrier downgrades below A-?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Hired & Non-Owned Auto Coverage
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard requirement for any business with employees driving personal/rental vehicles for business purposes.
findings.policy_quote: Hired auto: Class code 6611, $185 liability premium, AZ. Non-owned auto: Class code 6602, 55 employees, $73 premium, AZ.
findings.gap_description: Hired & Non-Owned Auto coverage confirmed in place. Important for election technology employees who travel between county offices using rental cars or personal vehicles.
findings.plain_english: Hired and non-owned auto coverage is in place — meaning when employees rent cars for travel or use personal vehicles for business, your auto policy responds. Good.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Consider increasing if employee count grows.

findings.requirement_type: Workers' Comp — Experience Modification Rate
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard credit for safety performance.
findings.policy_quote: EMR of 0.690 effective 04/01/2025 represents 31% below expected losses — excellent safety record. AZ also carries Schedule Modification of 0.750.
findings.gap_description: EMR of 0.690 is exceptional — 31% below the industry baseline of 1.00. Combined with AZ Schedule Mod of 0.750, the company realizes $21,611 in AZ credits alone. AR at 0.660 is also favorable. Significant signal of safety culture.
findings.plain_english: Your workers' comp experience modifier is 0.69 — meaning you have 31% fewer losses than the industry average for your work. That's excellent. It saves you real money and signals to county clients that you run a safe operation.
findings.recommendation: Maintain safety culture. Use the favorable EMR as a competitive differentiator in RFP responses (many counties require EMR ≤ 1.0).

findings.requirement_type: GL & Auto — Blanket Additional Insured + Primary & Noncontributory
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard government contract requirement: blanket AI status with primary & noncontributory wording.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL: 421-2915 Section (1) blanket AI by written contract, Section (2) primary & noncontributory; 421-0452 standalone P&NC. Auto: 461-0478 12 12 blanket AI + P&NC.
findings.gap_description: Blanket AI and P&NC are confirmed on both GL and Auto policies — contract-triggered (no scheduling required). Good structure for government contract compliance. Caveat: GL blanket AI excludes professional services claims (see finding-001 cluster); county clients are AI for premises/operations only, not for technology/service-failure claims.
findings.plain_english: Your GL and auto policies will automatically add counties as additional insureds whenever a contract requires it, with primary and noncontributory wording — meaning your coverage pays first and doesn't try to share with the county's own insurance. This is what government contracts demand. Good. The one caveat: counties are AI for slip-and-fall claims, not for election service failures (those are professional liability).
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Train COI processing team on the trigger requirements (must have written contract with the AI requirement).

findings.requirement_type: WC — Stop Gap for Monopolistic States
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for a multi-state employer: stop-gap EL coverage for monopolistic states (ND, OH, WA, WY).
findings.policy_quote: Stop Gap Employers' Liability coverage for ND, OH, WA, WY provided via WC 99 03 01 B Broad Form Endorsement.
findings.gap_description: Stop-gap coverage in place for the four monopolistic states where state-fund WC is mandatory. Protects against EL gap when employees travel to those states.
findings.plain_english: There are four states (North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, Wyoming) that require workers' comp from a state fund — your private policy can't write WC there. But your private policy DOES include 'stop gap' employers' liability coverage in those four states, so if an employee gets injured there and sues, you're protected. Good.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Confirm any expansion into those states is reported.

findings.requirement_type: PE Co-Defendant Extension on Management Liability
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation for PE-backed companies: PE sponsor protected as co-defendant when sued solely due to ownership/control.
findings.policy_quote: Named Co-Defendants: Lincoln Shields, LLC and Black Mountain Investment Company, LLC (the PE owners). Extends coverage to these PE entities and their affiliated holding vehicles, directors, officers, and employees when sued as co-defendants alongside an insured solely because of their ownership/management of Run-Test.
findings.gap_description: PE Co-Defendant Extension named both PE sponsors. When a third party sues the company and pulls the PE sponsors in solely as owners, the policy responds. Good structural fit for PE-backed company.
findings.plain_english: Your PE owners (Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain) are protected by your D&O if someone sues them solely because they own you. Good. They probably also have their own insurance, but yours is a useful first line.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Verify named entities still match current ownership at each renewal.

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice to Designated Government Entities
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard government contract requirement: 30-day advance cancellation notice to specified contract holders.
findings.policy_quote: 30-day advance cancellation notice to: El Paso County (CO), Coconino County (AZ), Amazon.com Services LLC, San Luis Obispo County (CA), City of Boulder, State of Colorado, NY State Office of General Services.
findings.policy_page: WC pg 112; Auto pgs 44-46; Property pg 36
findings.gap_description: Cancellation notice endorsements in place across multiple major contract counterparties. Good evidence of broker working closely with operations to keep contracts compliant.
findings.plain_english: When your insurance is cancelled, the policies will automatically notify your major county clients 30 days ahead. That meets standard government contract requirements. Make sure new contracts get added to this list as they're signed.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Establish quarterly process to update designated entities list as new contracts are won.

findings.requirement_type: Property — Equipment Breakdown Limit Adequacy
findings.contract_quote: Industry-standard expectation: meaningful Equipment Breakdown coverage for technology and printing operations.
findings.policy_quote: Property Equipment Breakdown $49,040,381; BI/EE extends existing limits; Data Restoration $100,000; Spoilage $100,000.
findings.gap_description: Equipment Breakdown limit at $49M is well-sized to printing presses, sorting equipment, and IT infrastructure. Service Interruption extension covers utility and cloud-computing service failures with 24-hour waiting period.
findings.plain_english: Your equipment breakdown insurance is $49 million — appropriate for industrial printing presses and sorting equipment. If a press blows up, you're well-covered for repair and lost income. Note one limitation: cyber-caused equipment damage isn't an 'accident' under this — that's why your cyber policy needs to handle it.
findings.recommendation: Maintain. Verify cloud-computing service interruption coverage covers all critical SaaS dependencies.
